title: Behavioural interview
blurb: STAR answers, conflict, ownership, mistakes and ambiguity, framed as 'which response lands best' so you can see why.

questions.q: Asked to describe a time you improved something, which ending gives the strongest Result in a STAR answer?
choices: "In the end the page was a lot faster and the whole team was really happy with it, so I think it went well."
"Load time fell from 4.1 to 1.2 seconds and the support tickets about it stopped. I learned to measure first."
"We shipped it on time after a lot of hard work from everyone, and my manager praised it at the sprint review."
"I used new techniques like caching and lazy loading that I had wanted to try, so I learned a great deal."
questions.why: A Result should be something the interviewer could verify: a number, a before and after, and what you took away. "A lot faster and everyone was happy" has no measure. "Shipped on time with praise" reports effort and approval, not the effect of the change. The techniques answer describes what you enjoyed, not what the improvement achieved.
questions.asked: Interviewers score the Result hardest because it is where vague candidates run out of detail.

questions.q: Which answer makes the candidate's own contribution clearest?
choices: "We noticed the import was failing, so we dug into the logs, found the encoding bug and fixed it all together."
"The team struggled with the import, and it was a great example of everyone pitching in to fix it."
"I traced the failing import to an encoding bug in the CSV parser, then wrote the fix and a regression test."
"The import had an encoding bug that broke about a third of uploads, and it was fixed in the next release."
questions.why: The interviewer is hiring you, not your team, so they need to hear what you did, with verbs they can ask about. The "we" answer hides whether you found the bug or watched. The team-spirit answer praises collaboration without a single action. The passive answer has a good measure but nobody doing anything. Crediting others is fine once your own part is clear.
questions.asked: A standard probe: if every sentence is "we", the next question is "what did you personally do?".

questions.q: The interviewer asks for "a quick example" of working under pressure. Which answer best fits the time you have?
choices: "On launch day our payment provider failed; I switched to the fallback, posted updates, and we lost no orders."
"First I need to explain how our team was structured in 2023, then how the migration plan changed over time."
"I work well under pressure in general: I stay calm, prioritise what matters and communicate with my team."
"There are a few: the launch, the migration, the audit last year and that outage, which were all stressful."
questions.why: "Quick" means one story with situation, action and result in a few sentences, which you can expand if asked. The background-first answer spends the time on context and may never reach an action. The general claim has no example at all, which is what the question asked for. Listing four stories without telling one shows no depth.
questions.asked: Tests whether you can size an answer to the question; rambling is one of the most common behavioural-round failures.

questions.q: Asked about "a technical challenge", which choice of story gives the interviewer the most to probe?
choices: "The tutorial app I built to learn React, since it was my first time using hooks and it was really hard."
"Our big platform migration, since it was the largest project the company ran, though I joined near the end."
"A bug that turned out to be a typo, since it shows how persistent I am when a problem takes a long time."
"The flaky checkout test I found was a race condition, since I can explain my reasoning, fix and trade-offs."
questions.why: A good story is one where you made the decisions and can defend them under follow-up questions. The tutorial was hard for you but has no real stakes. The migration is impressive, but you joined late, so the probing will expose how little you drove. The typo story shows persistence but no technical reasoning to discuss.
questions.asked: Story selection is half the answer; interviewers follow up on whatever you pick, so pick something you owned.

questions.q: Which answer best shows you can disagree productively with a more senior engineer?
choices: "I raised my concern once, but they were senior, so I went along with the design and kept my doubts quiet."
"I explained in the team channel why their design was wrong, several people agreed, and so they changed it."
"I wrote a one-page comparison with a benchmark, walked them through it, and we trialled my idea on one endpoint."
"I built my version on a branch over the weekend without telling them, so the results could speak for themselves."
questions.why: Productive disagreement brings evidence, in private, and proposes a cheap way to find out who is right. Staying quiet because of seniority withholds information the team needed. Winning in a public channel may get the result but damages the relationship. The secret weekend branch skips the conversation entirely and reads as going around a colleague.
questions.asked: Teams want people who push back with data and without drama; both silence and public point-scoring are red flags.

questions.q: Which answer best shows you can unblock a pull request without bypassing review?
choices: "I asked for a short call, understood their concern, split out the safe part to merge, and followed up on the rest."
"I asked our manager to overrule them, because the deadline mattered more than one reviewer's preferences."
"I made every change they asked for without discussion, even ones I thought were wrong, to avoid slowing us down."
"I found another reviewer who was happy to approve it as it was, merged it, and told the first one afterwards."
questions.why: The strong answer changes the channel from comments to conversation, finds the real concern and still ships something. Escalating to a manager first turns a technical question into a power question. Accepting every change silently avoids conflict but lets possibly wrong changes in. Reviewer-shopping bypasses the review process, which most teams treat as a serious breach of trust.
questions.asked: Code review friction is daily life; this checks you resolve it rather than escalate or route around it.

questions.q: The team chose an approach you argued against. Which answer best demonstrates disagree-and-commit?
choices: "I built it their way but kept a list of every problem it caused, so I could show at the retro that I had been right."
"I built it their way and said nothing more, since raising a decision again only slows the team and hurts morale."
"I agreed in the meeting but quietly kept my design in a separate module, so we could switch over if theirs failed."
"I said I still preferred my option, then built theirs properly and proposed a metric to check after a month."
questions.why: Disagree-and-commit means your dissent is on record, then you execute the decision fully, and you agree how to learn whether it worked. Keeping a list to prove yourself right is commitment in name only. Staying silent forever confuses committing with never revisiting. Hiding your own design in a module undermines the decision while pretending to support it.
questions.asked: Senior-leaning question; the metric-to-revisit detail is what separates a mature answer from compliance.

questions.q: Which answer best demonstrates ownership of an outage you caused?
choices: "Checkout went down after a deploy; a config value was wrong, which our review process should have caught."
"My config change took checkout down; I rolled back in ten minutes, said it was mine, and added a validation check."
"I made a mistake with a config change and felt terrible for weeks, so now I'm extremely careful with deploys."
"The outage was short and hit only a few users, so in the end it was not a big deal for the business overall."
questions.why: Ownership is saying "mine" early, fixing the immediate problem fast, and preventing a repeat with a mechanism rather than a promise. Blaming the review process shifts responsibility, even if the process also failed. Feeling terrible and "being careful" is emotion plus intention, with no fix. Minimising the impact dodges the question the interviewer actually asked.
questions.asked: Everyone breaks production eventually; the interviewer wants to know what you do in the first hour and the week after.

questions.q: Midway through a sprint you realise you will miss a deadline. Which answer best shows ownership?
choices: "I worked late every night to try to make it, and told the team on the last day that it wasn't quite done."
"I kept my head down and delivered two days late with high quality, which mattered more than the date."
"On day three I told my lead it would slip two days, explained why, and offered to cut the export to keep the date."
"I told the team the estimate had been unrealistic, since I hadn't been part of the planning session for it."
questions.why: Bad news early, with a reason and options, lets others re-plan while there is still time. Working late and revealing the slip on the last day removes every option except "late". Delivering late without warning assumes the date did not matter to anyone else. Blaming the estimate may be fair, but it is not ownership of what happens next.
questions.asked: Managers care less that estimates slip than about when they find out; this is the most common ownership probe.

questions.q: You find a bug in code a colleague wrote. Which answer best demonstrates ownership?
choices: "I told the colleague it was their code and their bug, so they should fix it when they had time, and moved on."
"I fixed it quietly in my own branch without mentioning it, since pointing out a mistake can feel awkward."
"I raised it in the retro as an example of why we need stricter reviews, so that everyone could learn from it."
"I wrote a failing test, fixed it, and added the colleague as a reviewer with a note on the cause for context."
questions.why: Owning the product means fixing what you find, whoever wrote it, and bringing the author along so they learn the cause. Handing it back as "their bug" leaves users exposed while it waits. A silent fix deprives the colleague of the lesson and hides a pattern. Using it as a retro example turns one bug into public blame.
questions.asked: Tests whether you think in terms of "our code" and can fix things without making it personal.

questions.q: Which answer best shows follow-through after an incident review?
choices: "The postmortem produced five action items that we all agreed mattered, so I'm sure most got done eventually."
"I suggested a follow-up meeting in a month to discuss whether the action items were still relevant to us."
"I wrote a detailed postmortem covering every step of the timeline, which the team said was very thorough."
"I took the alerting action item, gave it a date, shipped it next sprint, and closed the loop in the channel."
questions.why: Follow-through is visible completion: an owner, a date, the thing shipped and people told. "I'm sure most got done" admits nobody tracked them. A thorough document is useful, but writing it is not the same as changing anything. Scheduling a meeting to discuss relevance postpones the work and invites it to be dropped.
questions.asked: Postmortems whose actions never land are a known failure mode; interviewers look for people who close loops.

questions.q: You spot a security hole in a colleague's code that shipped last week. Which answer best demonstrates ownership?
choices: "I told my lead and the colleague privately that day, checked the logs for abuse, and we paired on a fix."
"I posted the details in the busy team channel straight away so that everyone could check their own code for it."
"I left a comment on the merged pull request describing it, so the author would see it when they next logged in."
"I waited for the next security audit, since the auditors are better placed to judge how serious it really is."
questions.why: A live vulnerability needs the right people told the same day, a check on whether it was exploited, and a fix, handled quietly. Posting details in a busy channel spreads an exploitable weakness further than needed. A comment on a merged PR may not be read for days. Waiting for an audit leaves users exposed for weeks.
questions.asked: Combines urgency, discretion and teamwork; how you raise it matters as much as that you do.

questions.q: Which answer best shows you can resolve an unclear requirement at the lowest cost?
choices: "I built what I thought they meant, since asking too many questions makes you look like you don't get it."
"I waited until the product owner rewrote the ticket in full detail, since a vague ticket wastes time."
"I built all three interpretations behind feature flags, so whichever they meant would be ready to ship."
"I wrote down my assumptions and two examples, confirmed them with the product owner, then built it."
questions.why: Writing assumptions down and checking them costs minutes and turns ambiguity into a decision someone signed off. Guessing to avoid looking uninformed risks building the wrong thing. Waiting for a perfect ticket stalls work and pushes your job onto someone else. Building every interpretation triples the work to avoid one conversation.
questions.asked: Real tickets are always vague; interviewers want to hear that you clarify cheaply and early.

questions.q: You join a team whose stack you have never used. Which answer best shows you can get productive fast?
choices: "I read the official docs cover to cover for two weeks before touching the code, so I understood it first."
"I asked my manager for a training course first, since learning on the job leads to bad habits later."
"I rewrote a small service in the stack I already knew to prove it would be faster, then offered to migrate."
"I picked a small bug in week one, traced it end to end with a teammate, and noted my questions as I went."
questions.why: Learning through a small real change with a guide gives feedback within days and touches the actual codebase and deploy path. Two weeks of reading delays any contribution and teaches the docs, not this code. Rewriting in your old stack avoids learning and creates a second stack to maintain. Waiting for a course puts your ramp-up on someone else's schedule.
questions.asked: Most hires land in an unfamiliar codebase; the interviewer wants a concrete learning method, not enthusiasm.

questions.q: In the interview you are asked a technical question you cannot answer. Which response gives the interviewer the most to assess?
choices: "I'm not sure. I haven't worked with that, so I can't really say anything useful. Could we move on?"
"I haven't used it, but I'd guess it works like connection pooling; I'd check by reading up and testing it."
"Great question. It's something every good developer should know, and it's on my list to read up on."
"Yes, I know that well: it's basically a cache, and we used something like it at my last company."
questions.why: Saying you do not know, then reasoning aloud from something related and naming how you would confirm it, shows how you work on the job. Stopping at "I don't know" gives the interviewer nothing to assess. Praising the question fills time without an answer. Bluffing is the worst option, because the follow-up question exposes it and costs your credibility on everything else.
questions.asked: Every interview hits a gap; interviewers are testing honesty and reasoning, not whether you know everything.

questions.q: Which answer best shows you can act on critical feedback?
choices: "My lead said my PRs were too big. I asked for an example, kept them under 300 lines, and checked back a month on."
"My lead said my PRs were too big, but I explained the features were complex, and they understood in the end."
"My lead said my PRs were too big. I thanked them, since feedback is a gift, and I always try to stay open to it."
"My lead said my PRs were too big, which surprised me, so I asked the rest of the team whether they agreed."
questions.why: Acting on feedback means clarifying it, changing something measurable, and checking whether the change worked. Explaining why the feedback was wrong is defending, not listening. Thanking them and "staying open" is the right attitude with no change attached. Polling the team for agreement treats the feedback as a vote rather than information.
questions.asked: Coachability is one of the main things a behavioural round screens for.

questions.q: Which answer best shows you can give a peer difficult feedback?
choices: "I mentioned it to our manager for their next one-to-one, since giving that sort of feedback is really their job."
"I told them privately that in two reviews their comments read as dismissive, quoted one, and asked their intent."
"I left it, because they are very experienced and I assumed they already knew how their comments came across."
"I raised review tone in the retro as a general point without naming anyone, so nobody would feel singled out."
questions.why: Good peer feedback is direct, private, specific (a quoted example) and curious about intent. Routing it through the manager avoids the conversation and can feel like a report. Saying nothing assumes they know, which they usually do not. A general retro point without names is so indirect that the person it concerns rarely recognises themselves.
questions.asked: Mid-level engineers are expected to give feedback, not only receive it; specificity is what interviewers listen for.

questions.q: Which answer best shows mentoring that builds a junior developer's independence?
choices: "When they got stuck I took the keyboard and fixed it quickly, since that saved time and they could read my commit."
"I sent them a list of good books and courses, and told them to come to me with any questions about anything."
"I paired on their first ticket, let them drive the second while I asked questions, and we reviewed each Friday."
"I reviewed their PRs very thoroughly and left detailed comments on every issue, so they saw every problem at once."
questions.why: Effective mentoring hands over control step by step and builds in regular reflection. Taking the keyboard solves today's problem and teaches dependence. A reading list plus "ask me anything" puts all the initiative on the person least able to take it. Exhaustive PR comments are feedback without guidance on what matters most, and often overwhelm.
questions.asked: Signals readiness for a senior role; the interviewer wants a method, not "I am always available".

questions.q: Asked "Why do you want to work here?", which answer shows the most genuine, specific interest?
choices: "You're a well-known company with a great reputation, and working here would look really good on my CV."
"I've heard great things about your culture, and the benefits and hybrid working are what I'm after."
"Your API docs taught me webhooks, and your Postgres migration post is exactly the work I want to do."
"I'm passionate about technology and love learning new things, so a fast-moving company suits me."
questions.why: A convincing answer names something only this company has and connects it to what you want to do. The reputation-and-CV answer is about what the company does for you. Culture and benefits are generic and true of many employers. Passion for technology could be said to any tech company, so it shows no research at all.
questions.asked: Checks that you did your homework; a specific reason is easy to prepare and rare to hear.

questions.q: At the end you are invited to ask questions. Which question best helps you judge whether the role suits you?
choices: "How much holiday do I get, and how soon after starting could I take time off for a trip I've planned?"
"I think you've covered everything really well, thank you, so I don't have any questions right now."
"What does a typical week look like in this role, and how does work get from a ticket into production?"
"What does your company actually do, and which of its products matter most to the business right now?"
questions.why: Asking about the day-to-day and the delivery path tells you about the work, the tooling and the team's maturity, and signals that you are thinking about doing the job. Holiday questions belong to the offer stage. Having no questions reads as low interest. Asking what the company does reveals you did not research it.
questions.asked: Your questions are assessed too; a good one shows you are evaluating the role, not only hoping to be picked.

questions.q: Two stakeholders each say their request is the most urgent and you can only do one this week. Which answer best shows you can prioritise without simply picking the louder voice?
choices: "I did the one whose stakeholder had asked first, since first come first served is the fairest rule and avoids arguments."
"I put both to my lead and the two stakeholders with the cost of each delay, and we agreed which shipped first."
"I worked evenings to deliver both, since choosing between stakeholders is not really a developer's decision to make."
"I started both so each stakeholder saw progress, then finished whichever one was closer to done at the end of the week."
questions.why: Prioritising means making the trade-off visible to the people who own it, with the cost of each option, and getting a decision rather than absorbing the conflict. First-come is a rule, not a judgement: it ignores impact entirely. Working evenings hides the capacity problem this week and sets up the same clash next week. Starting both spreads effort so that neither is done, and 'closer to done' is a decision made by accident.
questions.asked: Competing asks are weekly life for a mid-level developer; interviewers want to see the conflict escalated with data, not resolved by fatigue.

questions.q: Asked "Tell me about yourself", which opening best connects your background to this role in under a minute?
choices: "I was born in Leeds, studied history, and have had quite a few jobs, and I will walk you through each of them in order."
"I build full-stack CRUD apps in React and ASP.NET Core; most recently I cut our order screen's load time by 60%."
"I am a hard-working, passionate team player who loves learning new things and always gives one hundred per cent."
"Honestly, it is all on my CV, but in short I code, and I am looking for something new with better prospects."
questions.why: A good opener is a headline: what you do, in the stack they hire for, with one concrete result they can ask about. The chronological life story spends the minute on things the interviewer does not need. The adjectives answer claims qualities without evidence. Pointing at the CV and 'better prospects' gives nothing to probe and sounds disengaged.
questions.asked: The first answer sets the tone, and interviewers often pick their follow-ups from it.

questions.q: Which Situation line sets up a STAR story most efficiently?
choices: "Our checkout had a 9% failure rate on mobile, costing about £4k a week, and I owned the payment form."
"So, this was at my second job, which was a fintech, well sort of, and the team was about ten people I think."
"There was a problem with the website that was quite bad, and people were not happy about it at all."
"Let me explain our whole architecture first, starting with the load balancer and the six services behind it."
questions.why: The Situation should give just enough context to understand the stakes: what was wrong, why it mattered, and your role, in one or two sentences. The rambling company history uses time without establishing stakes. 'Quite bad' has no measure or role. Explaining the whole architecture buries the problem before the story has started.
questions.asked: Most candidates overspend on the Situation; interviewers notice when you get to the point.

questions.q: Which Action section best shows the reasoning behind what you did, not just the steps?
choices: "I added an index on customer_id, deployed it, then checked the dashboards, and that fixed the slow page."
"I did what any good developer would do and optimised it properly, following all the best practices I knew."
"I tried lots of different things over a couple of weeks until something eventually made the page load faster."
"I profiled first, saw 80% of time was one query, and indexed it; caching was no use as the data changed often."
questions.why: Interviewers assess judgement, so the strongest Action says what evidence you gathered and why you chose one option over another. The step list shows what you did but not why an index rather than a cache. 'Lots of things' suggests trial and error. 'Best practices' is a claim with no content to probe.
questions.asked: The 'why' inside the Action is what separates mid-level answers from junior ones.

questions.q: After your story the interviewer asks "What would you do differently?" Which answer shows the most useful reflection?
choices: "Nothing really. It went well, we hit the date, and I would make exactly the same decisions again."
"I would have worked longer hours earlier on, so that we would have had more buffer at the end."
"I would agree the API contract with the mobile team in week one; late changes cost us four days."
"I would probably have had a better manager, because a lot of the problems came from above me."
questions.why: A strong reflection names a specific decision, what it cost and what you would change, which shows you learn from experience. 'Nothing' suggests you do not review your own work. Working longer hours is effort, not a better process. Blaming the manager puts the lesson on someone else and is a red flag in any interview.
questions.asked: Almost every behavioural story gets this follow-up, so prepare a real answer for each one.

questions.q: Asked "Tell me about a project you are proud of", which answer makes your impact and your role clearest?
choices: "I am proud of our booking app, which used React, Redux, Node, Postgres, Docker and a CI pipeline."
"I led our booking-flow rewrite and designed the slot locking; double bookings fell from ten a week to none."
"Our team built a booking app that everyone liked, and it was really fun to work on with such great people."
"The booking app was a big project for the company and took about eight months from start to finish."
questions.why: Pride should be backed by what you personally did and what changed because of it, in a way the interviewer can probe. The tech list shows tools, not impact or role. The team answer is warm but says nothing about you or the result. The size and duration answer describes the project, not your contribution.
questions.asked: An open question that rewards candidates who lead with their own impact.

questions.q: Asked for "a time you failed", which answer picks a failure of the right size and shows real learning?
choices: "A migration I shipped untested on real data locked the orders table for ten minutes. Now I rehearse on a copy."
"I sometimes care too much about quality, so a feature once took a little longer than we planned."
"The whole project failed because the client kept changing requirements, so there was not much I could do."
"I once deleted the entire production database with no backups, and the company nearly went under."
questions.why: A good failure story is real, owned, moderate in size and ends with a changed habit. The 'care too much' answer is a disguised boast that interviewers see through. The client answer blames others and has no lesson. The catastrophic story raises questions about judgement that one interview answer cannot settle, and says nothing about what changed.
questions.asked: Interviewers want evidence of self-awareness; a humblebrag is marked lower than an honest small mistake.

questions.q: Describing a failed project, which answer best avoids blame while staying honest about what went wrong?
choices: "The PM gave us awful requirements and QA missed everything, so honestly it was doomed before I joined."
"Nobody did anything wrong as such; sometimes projects just fail and there is no real reason for it."
"It failed, but it was not my part that failed, since my backend work was finished and fully tested."
"We skipped user research, and I did not voice my doubts. Now we test ideas with prototypes first."
questions.why: Honest post-project reflection names the real causes, including your share, and what the team changed. Blaming the PM and QA shows no ownership. 'Projects just fail' dodges the question and has no lesson. Separating your part from the failure suggests you think of success as your tickets rather than the outcome.
questions.asked: How you talk about other people's mistakes predicts how you will talk about your new colleagues.

questions.q: Asked about going "above and beyond", which answer best shows good judgement rather than heroics?
choices: "I worked three all-nighters in a row to ship on time, and I barely slept that whole week, but we made it."
"I always do more than I am asked, because that is just the kind of person that I have always been."
"I noticed backups had never been test-restored, tried one, found it broken, and set up a monthly check."
"I rewrote the whole frontend over a weekend without telling anyone, and it was much better afterwards."
questions.why: The strongest 'above and beyond' story is noticing a risk outside your ticket and fixing it sustainably. All-nighters show commitment but also poor planning and an unsustainable pace. The character claim has no evidence. A secret weekend rewrite ignores the team, review and risk, which many interviewers treat as a warning sign.
questions.asked: Interviewers are wary of hero stories; they want initiative that the team can rely on.

questions.q: The interviewer says "Give me the one-line version first." Which headline best sets up a story about a performance fix?
choices: "It is a long story, so let me start with some background on the company and the product first."
"I found an N+1 query on our dashboard and cut its load time from 8 seconds to under 1 second."
"It was about performance, which is something I am very interested in and have read a lot about."
"I think it went well, but I am not sure the metric I used was the right one, so it is hard to say."
questions.why: Leading with the result tells the interviewer where the story goes and lets them steer the detail. Starting with background ignores the request. The interest answer talks about you instead of the event. Opening with self-doubt undercuts the story before it starts; nuance belongs in the reflection, not the headline.
questions.asked: Headline-first answers are easy to follow and easy to score, which interviewers appreciate.

questions.q: The product manager wants a feature you believe will hurt performance. Which answer best shows you can disagree using evidence?
choices: "I prototyped it, showed it added 900 ms on mobile, and proposed lazy-loading it; the PM agreed."
"I built it as asked, since the PM decides, even though I was fairly sure it would slow the page."
"I told the PM it was a bad idea, and I refused to build it until they changed their mind about it."
"I complained to my manager, who then spoke to the PM for me, and the feature was eventually dropped."
questions.why: Evidence plus an alternative turns a disagreement into a shared decision. Refusing to build puts you in a standoff over a call that is not yours alone. Building silently avoids conflict but hides a risk you saw. Escalating to your manager without talking to the PM first damages the relationship and skips the cheapest route.
questions.asked: Interviewers look for disagreement that is direct, evidence-based and leaves the relationship intact.

questions.q: You and a teammate keep leaving each other opposing style comments in reviews. Which answer best shows a lasting fix?
choices: "I kept commenting, because if I stopped they would think they were right, and the code would suffer."
"I started approving their PRs without style comments, so that they would do the same thing for mine."
"I asked our lead to tell them that my style was correct, since I had more experience with the codebase."
"I proposed we let the formatter and linter decide, got the team to agree a config, and the comments stopped."
questions.why: A recurring dispute is fixed by changing the system, here by handing style to tools the whole team agrees on. A private truce removes the friction but leaves the code inconsistent. Asking the lead to rule for you turns a team question into a win-lose. Continuing the fight keeps wasting review time.
questions.asked: Shows whether you look for a structural fix or just win arguments.

questions.q: A teammate keeps missing agreed deadlines and it is delaying your work. Which answer best shows a direct, respectful approach?
choices: "I raised it with our manager straight away so they could deal with it, since it was not my job."
"I quietly did their tasks myself in the evenings, so the team would not miss the sprint goal."
"I asked them privately how things were going, learned they were stuck, and we paired to unblock it."
"I mentioned it at stand-up in front of everyone so that there was some pressure on them to improve."
questions.why: Starting with a private, curious conversation often reveals a cause you can help with, and escalation stays available. Going straight to the manager skips that and damages trust. Covering their work hides the problem and burns you out. Calling someone out at stand-up embarrasses them and rarely changes behaviour.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to see you assume good intent and talk to people before escalating.

questions.q: A colleague presented your work in a demo as theirs. Which answer best shows professional handling?
choices: "I interrupted the demo and told everyone that I was actually the one who had built that feature."
"I spoke to them privately about it, and after that we agreed to both name who built what in demos."
"I posted in the team channel that some people like taking credit for things they did not do."
"I said nothing, since credit does not really matter as long as the work gets shipped in the end."
questions.why: A private conversation assumes it may have been careless rather than malicious, and agreeing a norm stops it recurring. Interrupting the demo creates a public confrontation. Saying nothing lets it continue and can hurt your own visibility at review time. A passive-aggressive post damages trust with the whole team.
questions.asked: Tests maturity: can you protect your interests without a public fight?

questions.q: Your manager sets a deadline you believe is unrealistic. Which answer best shows you can raise the risk constructively?
choices: "I broke the work down, showed what could fit by that date, and offered two options for the remainder."
"I told them the date was impossible and that they clearly did not understand how software works."
"I said yes to keep them happy, then worked every weekend to hit the date without telling anyone."
"I agreed to the date, and when we missed it I explained that I had always thought it was unrealistic."
questions.why: Turning 'this is unrealistic' into a breakdown and options gives the manager real choices: cut scope, move the date or add risk. Saying yes and working weekends hides the problem and is unsustainable. Calling the date impossible without detail sounds like a refusal. Saying 'I told you so' afterwards is the worst of both.
questions.asked: Deadline pressure is universal; interviewers want to know you will warn early with options.

questions.q: In a design review, you and a senior colleague favour different databases. Which answer best shows you kept the discussion on criteria?
choices: "I let them choose, then pointed out the problems with their choice later on once they showed up."
"I deferred straight away, because they were more senior and had probably thought about it more."
"I argued for my choice until the end of the meeting, since I was sure that it was the better option."
"I suggested we agree what mattered most, then scored both options on it, and theirs came out ahead."
questions.why: Agreeing the criteria first (consistency, team skills, hosting cost) takes ego out of the choice, and accepting a result that goes against you shows the method is genuine. Deferring on seniority alone withholds your view. Arguing to the end is about winning. Saving criticism for later is disagreement without the courage to raise it.
questions.asked: A strong answer shows you care more about the decision than about being right.

questions.q: A reviewer leaves a sharp, dismissive comment on your PR. Which answer best shows you can de-escalate?
choices: "I replied in the thread pointing out that their own code had the same issue in several other places."
"I made every change they asked for without discussing it, just to get the PR merged quickly."
"I suggested a quick call, asked what worried them, and we agreed a change that addressed it."
"I reported the comment to HR, since that tone should never be acceptable at any workplace."
questions.why: Moving a tense thread to a short call removes tone from the equation, and asking about the underlying concern usually shows it was reasonable. Pointing at their code escalates. Silently complying avoids conflict but may accept a worse change and leaves the tone unaddressed. HR is for serious or repeated conduct, not a first sharp comment.
questions.asked: Written review tone causes more friction than code; interviewers want to see you handle it.

questions.q: Two teammates are arguing over whose approach to use and the work is stalled. Which answer best shows you can facilitate?
choices: "I picked the approach I liked best and started building it, so that the argument would just end."
"I had each list pros and cons, we timeboxed a spike on the riskiest part, and the result decided it."
"I stayed out of it, since it was their disagreement and not my place to get involved in any way."
"I asked the manager to choose for them, because a decision from above settles things more quickly."
questions.why: Facilitation gives both people a fair process and a way to decide on evidence, so nobody simply loses. Picking your own approach adds a third opinion and bypasses them. Staying out lets the team stall. Asking the manager to choose may be needed eventually but skips steps the team can take itself.
questions.asked: Mid-level engineers are expected to unstick team decisions, not just their own work.

questions.q: A bug you approved in code review reaches production. Which answer best shows ownership as the reviewer?
choices: "I helped fix it, then admitted I had skimmed a large PR, and now I ask for big changes to be split."
"The author wrote the bug, so it was their responsibility; reviewers cannot be expected to catch everything."
"I reviewed it properly, so the problem must have been the tests, which is QA's area rather than mine."
"I felt bad about it, so from then on I stopped reviewing PRs in areas that I did not know well."
questions.why: Approving is a shared responsibility, so ownership means helping fix it, naming what you did wrong and changing your practice. Putting it all on the author ignores what approval means. Blaming QA shifts the fault again. Withdrawing from unfamiliar reviews removes a reviewer instead of improving how you review.
questions.asked: Many candidates only own code they wrote; owning your reviews shows a team mindset.

questions.q: A flaky test that no one owns fails a third of CI runs. Which answer best shows initiative?
choices: "I just re-ran the pipeline whenever it failed, as everyone else did, and it usually passed on retry."
"I raised a ticket for the team that owns CI and told everyone to wait for them to fix it later."
"I disabled the test so CI would be green, since a flaky test is no better than having no test."
"I found it depended on test order, fixed the shared state, and added a CI report of flaky tests."
questions.why: Initiative is fixing the root cause of a shared problem and making the next one visible. Re-running is the habit that lets flakiness spread. Disabling hides a test that may be catching a real race. A ticket to another team is reasonable only if you cannot fix it, and 'wait' leaves everyone blocked.
questions.asked: Interviewers love small, concrete initiative stories because they predict day-to-day behaviour.

questions.q: At 5 p.m. on a Friday you notice a bug that is double-charging some customers. Which answer best shows judgement?
choices: "I noted it for Monday, since nothing should be deployed on a Friday and the weekend is protected."
"I pushed a quick fix straight to production on my own, since there was no time to wait for review."
"I raised an incident, turned the feature off by its flag, and got a reviewed fix out that evening."
"I emailed the whole company about it so that everyone was aware, and then logged off for the weekend."
questions.why: Customer money is at stake, so you stop the harm fast (flag off), bring in others and still review the fix. Waiting until Monday lets customers be charged all weekend. An unreviewed Friday push risks making it worse. A company-wide email creates noise without anyone owning the fix.
questions.asked: Tests whether you balance urgency and safety when customers are affected.

questions.q: Your ticket passed review and was merged. Which answer best shows follow-through beyond the merge?
choices: "Once it was merged I moved straight on, since QA and ops handle everything after that point."
"I checked it in production, watched the error rate, and told the requester it was live."
"I closed the ticket immediately, since the definition of done only goes as far as the merge."
"I waited for users to report any problems, because they are the ones who really test features."
questions.why: Ownership continues until the change works for users: verifying in production, watching metrics and closing the loop with whoever asked. Handing off at merge assumes someone else will notice problems. A definition of done that stops at merge is one to question, and waiting for user reports means users find your bugs.
questions.asked: A small habit that marks a developer others trust with their features.

questions.q: You realise you promised a teammate an API change by Wednesday and will not make it. Which answer best shows reliable communication?
choices: "I told them on Monday as soon as I knew, gave a new date, and offered a stub they could build against."
"I kept working and delivered on Friday, since two days late is not a big deal in most projects."
"I told them on Wednesday afternoon that it had been more complicated than expected, sorry about that."
"I asked another developer to finish it for me without telling my teammate that anything had changed."
questions.why: Early warning lets others re-plan, and a stub reduces the damage. Delivering late without warning leaves the teammate blocked and guessing. Telling them on the deadline is too late to help. Quietly handing it off may work but hides the change and the risk from the person depending on you.
questions.asked: Reliability is less about never slipping and more about saying so early.

questions.q: Onboarding took you two weeks because setup steps were undocumented. Which answer best shows ownership of the problem?
choices: "I told my manager onboarding was poor, so that they could raise it with the team in the future."
"I asked a senior developer to set up my machine for me, and I avoided touching the setup after that."
"I accepted it, since every company has messy onboarding and new people always have to struggle."
"I wrote down each fix as I hit it, turned it into a setup script, and the next hire was ready in a day."
questions.why: New joiners are best placed to see onboarding gaps, and fixing them as you go helps the next person measurably. Reporting it to your manager passes the work on. Accepting it treats a fixable problem as normal. Having someone else set you up gets you working but leaves the gap for everyone after you.
questions.asked: Good for junior and mid candidates: it shows impact without needing seniority.

questions.q: A ticket says only "Make the dashboard faster." Which answer best shows you can turn vagueness into a clear goal?
choices: "I optimised everything I could find on the dashboard until it felt noticeably faster to me."
"I sent the ticket back, since I could not start work until someone wrote proper requirements."
"I asked which view felt slow and for whom, measured it at 6 s, and agreed a goal of under 2 s."
"I rebuilt the dashboard in a newer framework, since that was likely to make it faster overall."
questions.why: Clarifying who is affected, measuring the baseline and agreeing a target gives you a definition of done and a result to report. Optimising 'until it felt faster' has no target or measure. Bouncing the ticket back without questions stalls it. A framework rewrite is a large, risky guess about the cause.
questions.asked: Vague tickets are daily life; interviewers want to hear you ask questions and measure.

questions.q: Your manager and the product owner give you conflicting top priorities for the week. Which answer best shows you can resolve it?
choices: "I did the product owner's task, since product decides priorities, and told my manager afterwards."
"I put both requests in one message to them, explained I could do one, and asked them to agree which."
"I did whichever one I found more interesting, as both of them seemed to be equally important."
"I tried to do both at once, working late, so that neither of them would be disappointed in me."
questions.why: When two people with authority disagree, the fix is to make the conflict visible to both and let them decide, with your capacity stated plainly. Choosing one side yourself leaves the other surprised. Doing both by working late hides the conflict. Picking by interest ignores the business entirely.
questions.asked: Tests whether you surface conflicts instead of absorbing them silently.

questions.q: You inherit an undocumented legacy service and must change it. Which answer best shows a safe way to learn it?
choices: "I traced one real request through the logs, added tests around the part I changed, then refactored."
"I made the change and relied on users to tell us if anything broke, since there were no tests."
"I read every file from top to bottom first, so I understood all of it before changing anything."
"I proposed rewriting it from scratch, as old code without documentation is not worth learning."
questions.why: Following a real request shows how the system behaves, and characterisation tests pin that behaviour before you change it. Reading every file is slow and does not tell you which paths matter. Changing it untested pushes risk onto users. Proposing a rewrite before understanding it is the classic legacy mistake.
questions.asked: Legacy code is most of real work; interviewers want a method, not bravado.

questions.q: You are asked to deliver a feature in half the estimated time. Which answer best shows you can negotiate scope?
choices: "I said it could not be done and that the original estimate had to stand, whatever the business wanted."
"I agreed and cut the tests to save time, since tests could always be added in a later sprint."
"I agreed and asked for two more developers, since doubling the team would halve the time taken."
"I asked what mattered most by that date, proposed a smaller first release, and scheduled the rest."
questions.why: Finding the core need and shipping a smaller slice meets the business date without hiding risk. Refusing flatly ignores why the date matters. Cutting tests borrows against quality and rarely gets paid back. Adding people late usually slows a project down, because onboarding and coordination cost more than they add.
questions.asked: A negotiation question in disguise; interviewers want options, not yes or no.

questions.q: You are constantly interrupted by support questions during sprint work. Which answer best shows you improved the system?
choices: "I turned off chat notifications completely, so that nobody could interrupt my focus time again."
"I answered every question straight away, since helping people is always more important than tickets."
"I logged a week of questions, wrote an FAQ for the top five, and proposed a rotating support role."
"I asked my manager to tell support to stop contacting developers directly with their questions."
questions.why: Measuring the interruptions, removing the most common ones and sharing the rest across a rota fixes the cause for the whole team. Going dark shifts the problem to colleagues and support. Answering everything instantly sacrifices sprint work. Asking your manager to block support treats a real need as a nuisance.
questions.asked: Shows you can improve a team's working conditions with data, which is a mid-level expectation.

questions.q: Your lead tells you your pull requests are too big to review well. Which answer best shows you acted on the feedback?
choices: "I explained that my features are just naturally large, and that splitting them would slow me down a lot."
"I agreed, then kept opening large PRs but added longer descriptions, so they were easier to read."
"I started splitting work into refactor and behaviour PRs under 300 lines; review time halved."
"I thanked them for the feedback and said I would definitely try to keep it in mind going forward."
questions.why: Acting on feedback means a visible change in behaviour and some evidence it worked. Defending the habit shows you heard criticism rather than information. Longer descriptions address a different problem and leave the PRs just as hard to review. A polite promise to 'keep it in mind' has no action or result, so there is nothing to assess.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask for specific feedback you received, then listen for what you changed.

questions.q: You had to learn a framework you had never used within two weeks. Which answer best shows an effective learning method?
choices: "I read the official documentation cover to cover before writing a single line of code in it."
"I built a tiny version of our real feature, asked a colleague to review it, and read docs as I hit gaps."
"I watched a long video course on it at double speed, which covered everything I needed to know."
"I copied patterns from the existing codebase without really understanding them, and it mostly worked out."
questions.why: Learning by building something real, with fast feedback from someone who knows the stack, gets you productive quickest. Reading all the docs first delays practice and much of it will not stick. A video course is passive and not tied to your problem. Copying without understanding works until the first bug you cannot explain.
questions.asked: Every job needs you to learn fast; interviewers want a repeatable method.

questions.q: Asked how you keep your skills current, which answer gives the most concrete, credible evidence?
choices: "I read release notes for tools we use; after React 19 I moved our forms to actions and wrote it up."
"I follow lots of developers on social media and try to keep up with everything that is happening in tech."
"I am always learning, it is just part of who I am, and I really love technology in general."
"I have bookmarked hundreds of articles that I am planning to read when I get the time for it."
questions.why: Credible answers show a habit and an outcome: something you learned and applied at work. Following people on social media is passive and says nothing about what you did with it. A statement about who you are has no evidence. A backlog of unread bookmarks suggests intent rather than learning.
questions.asked: A common warm-up; a specific example beats a list of blogs every time.

questions.q: You receive feedback you think is unfair. Which answer best shows you can engage with it rather than dismiss it?
choices: "I ignored it, because I knew my work was good and they did not understand the context I was in."
"I accepted all of it without question, since the person giving feedback is usually right about it."
"I pointed out that they had made the same mistakes themselves, so they were not really in a position to say."
"I asked for a specific example, found part of it was fair, acted on that, and explained my view on the rest."
questions.why: Asking for examples turns a vague judgement into something you can assess, and acting on the fair part while explaining your view shows maturity. Accepting everything uncritically can lead you to change the wrong things. Turning it back on them is defensive. Ignoring it throws away information and damages the relationship.
questions.asked: Tests whether you are coachable without being a pushover.

questions.q: Which answer best shows you can give constructive feedback to your own manager?
choices: "I never give my manager feedback, since it is not really my place to criticise the person above me."
"I told the whole team at the retro that the manager's planning was poor, so that it would be on the record."
"In our one-to-one I said last-minute scope changes cost us two days, and asked if we could fix a cut-off."
"I sent an anonymous message through the survey tool, since telling them in person felt too risky."
questions.why: Good upward feedback is private, specific about impact and comes with a proposal. Never giving it leaves problems unaddressed. Raising it publicly in a retro puts the manager on the spot. An anonymous survey can be right when trust is low, but it is less specific and cannot start a conversation about a fix.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to know you will tell them when something is not working.

questions.q: Asked about a time you changed your mind, which answer best shows openness to evidence?
choices: "I rarely change my mind, because I research things carefully before forming any strong opinion."
"I was sure GraphQL was overkill, but a spike showed it removed six endpoints, so I backed the switch."
"I changed my mind when my manager told me to, since in the end it was their call and not mine."
"I change my mind all the time, because I like to stay flexible and I try not to hold any strong views."
questions.why: The strongest answer shows a firm view, new evidence, and a visible change of position. 'I rarely change my mind' signals rigidity. Changing because a manager said so is compliance, not persuasion. Changing constantly without strong views suggests you do not form judgements at all.
questions.asked: Intellectual honesty is hard to fake; interviewers use this to test for it.

questions.q: You have been stuck on a bug for a whole morning. Which answer best shows good judgement about asking for help?
choices: "I timebox it to about an hour, write up what I have tried, then ask someone with the right context."
"I ask for help as soon as I hit anything unfamiliar, so I do not waste any time at all."
"I kept going for three days, since asking would make me look like I did not know what I was doing."
"I never ask for help, because figuring things out alone is how you get better as a developer."
questions.why: A timebox balances learning with the team's time, and writing up what you tried makes the question quick to answer. Never asking wastes days on things a colleague knows in minutes. Asking at the first hurdle means you never build independence. Hiding struggles to look competent is what actually costs trust.
questions.asked: Juniors and mids are often judged on when they ask for help, not whether.

questions.q: You have to explain an outage to a non-technical sales director. Which answer best shows clear communication?
choices: "I explained the race condition between the two Kubernetes pods and the connection pool in detail."
"I forwarded them the whole incident channel so they could read for themselves everything that had happened."
"I said it was a technical issue that the engineering team had now fixed, and left it at that."
"I said orders failed for 40 minutes, about 200 customers were hit, and this cause is now fixed for good."
questions.why: Non-technical audiences need impact, scope and reassurance in their own terms. The deep technical explanation is accurate but not useful to them. 'A technical issue' is so vague it sounds evasive. Forwarding the raw incident channel makes them do the work of finding the story.
questions.asked: Mid-level developers talk to stakeholders; interviewers test whether you can translate.

questions.q: A designer hands you a layout that would take weeks to build as drawn. Which answer best shows productive collaboration?
choices: "I built exactly what was designed, since the design is the designer's decision and not mine."
"I built something simpler instead without asking, since they would not notice the difference."
"I showed them what was costly, suggested a near version using existing components, and we agreed it."
"I told them the design was unrealistic and that they should learn more about how the web works."
questions.why: Collaboration means sharing the cost of each part so the designer can make trade-offs, and offering an alternative. Building it all blindly spends weeks without anyone choosing to. Changing it silently breaks trust when they notice. Telling them to learn the web is dismissive and ends the conversation.
questions.asked: Frontend roles especially; interviewers want to see you treat design as a partnership.

questions.q: A tester keeps reopening your tickets for issues outside the acceptance criteria. Which answer best shows a collaborative fix?
choices: "I closed the reopened tickets again, since they were not part of what the story had asked for."
"I invited the tester to refinement so edge cases are agreed before build, and reopens dropped sharply."
"I fixed every one of them without comment, to avoid any arguments with the testing team."
"I asked my manager to tell the tester to stick strictly to the written acceptance criteria in future sprints."
questions.why: Bringing testing into refinement catches edge cases before development, which is the root cause of late reopens. Closing tickets again turns it into a tug of war. Fixing everything silently lets scope grow unchecked. Asking a manager to intervene is heavy-handed when a process change fixes it.
questions.asked: Shows you fix recurring friction with process rather than argument.

questions.q: Your team is split across London and Singapore with two hours of overlap. Which answer best shows effective remote collaboration?
choices: "I wrote clear hand-off notes each evening and saved the overlap for decisions that needed discussion."
"I sent quick chat messages whenever I needed something and waited for whenever they replied."
"I moved my working hours to overlap fully with Singapore, even though it meant working very late."
"I set up daily hour-long video calls for everyone, so that we were always fully in sync."
questions.why: Async hand-offs keep work moving across time zones, and the scarce overlap is spent on what really needs a conversation. Working very late is unsustainable. Fragmentary chat messages cause day-long round trips. Long daily calls consume most of the overlap on status that could be written.
questions.asked: Remote and distributed teams are the norm; interviewers want to see async habits.

questions.q: A new developer joins your team. Which answer best shows you helped them become productive quickly?
choices: "I sent them the wiki link on their first day and told them to come and ask me if anything was unclear."
"I did their first few tickets for them, so they could watch and learn how things were done here."
"I left them to explore on their own, since that is the best way to really learn a new codebase."
"I paired on their first ticket, gave them a small real bug next, and checked in daily for two weeks."
questions.why: Pairing first, then a small real task with regular check-ins, builds confidence and context quickly. A wiki link and 'ask me' puts all the effort on someone who does not know what to ask. Doing their tickets teaches little. Leaving them alone is slow and can feel unwelcoming.
questions.asked: Helping others ramp up is a common mid-level expectation.

questions.q: A salesperson promises a client a feature that does not exist, due next week. Which answer best shows you can push back constructively?
choices: "I built it over the weekend, since the client had already been promised it and we could not let them down."
"I told the salesperson it was their problem, since they should not have promised it in the first place."
"I took it to the product owner with a quick estimate and a smaller option we could offer by that date."
"I ignored it, as sales requests should come through the product owner rather than directly to me."
questions.why: Involving the product owner routes the decision correctly, and a smaller option gives sales something real to take back. Building it over the weekend rewards bypassing the process and burns you out. 'Their problem' damages a relationship you will need. Ignoring it leaves the client and the salesperson in trouble.
questions.asked: Tests whether you can protect the team's process while still helping the business.

questions.q: Your project is going to slip by two weeks. Which status update best shows honest, useful communication?
choices: "We are slightly behind, but I am confident we can catch up if everyone keeps working hard."
"Payments integration is two weeks late due to sandbox issues; options: cut refunds or move the date."
"Things are progressing and the team is making good headway on many of the key workstreams."
"The delay is entirely due to the payment provider, and there is really nothing we can do about it."
questions.why: A useful update states the size of the slip, the cause and the decisions the reader can make. 'Slightly behind but confident' hides a two-week gap. Vague progress language gives the reader nothing to act on. Blaming the provider without options leaves stakeholders stuck and sounds defensive.
questions.asked: Bad news delivered early with options builds more trust than good news that later turns out wrong.

questions.q: Your feature depends on another team who keep deprioritising your request. Which answer best shows cross-team influence?
choices: "I explained our deadline and its value to their lead, and offered to write the change for their review."
"I kept messaging them every day until they finally agreed to do it, just to get me to stop."
"I worked around their system entirely by duplicating their data in our own database instead."
"I escalated to their director on the very first day, since that is the only way to get anything done there."
questions.why: Influence without authority means explaining why it matters to them and lowering their cost, here by offering the change for their review. Daily nagging gets resentment. Duplicating their data creates a consistency problem that outlives the deadline. Escalating on day one skips the conversation and damages the relationship.
questions.asked: Mid-level engineers are expected to unblock themselves across team boundaries.

questions.q: Which answer best shows you led a small project without having formal authority?
choices: "I told the others what to work on each day, since somebody had to take charge of the project."
"I did all of the work myself so it would be done properly, and just kept the rest of the team updated on it."
"I waited for my manager to assign a lead, since leading without the title would not be respected."
"I wrote a one-page plan, agreed tasks with each person, ran a weekly check-in, and we shipped on time."
questions.why: Leading without authority works through a shared plan, agreement rather than orders, and a steady rhythm of check-ins. Telling people what to do without authority breeds resistance. Doing everything yourself is not leading and does not scale. Waiting for a title misses the chance to show you are ready for one.
questions.asked: The classic step from junior to mid-level; interviewers want concrete mechanics.

questions.q: You want your team to adopt automated end-to-end tests. Which answer best shows how you drove adoption?
choices: "I added a rule that every PR must have end-to-end tests, and blocked any PR that did not have one."
"I sent an article explaining why end-to-end tests are important, and hoped people would read it."
"I added tests for the checkout flow, showed the bug they caught, and paired with others on the next."
"I wrote all the tests myself over a month, since the team would never do it on their own anyway."
questions.why: Adoption comes from showing value on something people care about, then making it easy to join in. Imposing a blocking rule without buy-in creates resentment and hollow tests. An article without a demonstration changes little. Writing everything yourself builds a suite nobody else maintains.
questions.asked: Changing team habits is harder than writing code; interviewers want to see how you persuade.

questions.q: Which answer best shows you improved a team process with measurable effect?
choices: "I suggested we have more meetings to talk about problems, and people seemed to like the idea."
"I noticed reviews waited a day, proposed a morning review slot, and median wait fell to three hours."
"I improved lots of our processes, which made the team much more efficient in a number of ways."
"I changed our board columns around, and although nobody measured it I think it helped quite a bit."
questions.why: A strong process story has a measured problem, a specific change and a measured result. 'More meetings' is not an improvement by itself and 'seemed to like it' is not evidence. 'Lots of processes' gives the interviewer nothing to probe. An unmeasured board change may have helped, but you cannot show it did.
questions.asked: Interviewers look for developers who improve how the team works, not only what it ships.

questions.q: You made a technical decision that some teammates disliked. Which answer best shows you handled it well?
choices: "I explained the trade-offs I had weighed, listened to their concerns, and agreed a point to review it."
"I reversed the decision straight away, since keeping the team happy mattered more than the choice."
"I stuck with it and did not discuss it further, since the decision had already been made by then."
"I told them that if they disliked it they should have spoken up sooner, when it was being discussed."
questions.why: Explaining your reasoning, genuinely listening and agreeing when you will revisit it keeps trust while still making progress. Reversing instantly means decisions are set by whoever objects loudest. Refusing to discuss it makes people feel unheard. Blaming them for not speaking earlier is defensive, even if it is partly true.
questions.asked: Tests whether you can own an unpopular decision without either caving or bulldozing.

questions.q: You need to split a feature across three developers. Which answer best shows effective delegation?
choices: "I split it by layer, so one did the database, one the API and one the UI, and we joined it at the end."
"I gave the hardest parts to myself and the simple parts to the others, so nothing would go wrong."
"I let everyone pick whatever they wanted to work on, so they would all feel motivated and engaged."
"I defined the API contract first, split by user flow, and let each person own their slice end to end."
questions.why: Agreeing the contract first lets people work in parallel, and vertical slices give each person something that ships and that they own. Splitting by layer delays integration until the end, where the problems hide. Keeping the hard parts yourself stops others growing. Free choice without structure leaves gaps and overlaps.
questions.asked: Tests whether you can plan work for others, a key step towards senior.

questions.q: Asked about a mistake that affected customers, which answer shows the best balance of honesty and recovery?
choices: "I have been lucky enough never to make a mistake that reached customers in any of my jobs so far."
"There was a small issue once, but it was really more of a misunderstanding with the requirements."
"A cache bug I wrote showed one user's basket to another; I rolled back, we told them, and I added tests."
"I made a mistake, but my reviewer should have caught it too, so really the fault was shared between the two of us."
questions.why: Owning a real mistake, the immediate recovery, telling the people affected and the preventive change is what interviewers want. Claiming no customer-facing mistakes is either untrue or suggests little responsibility. Recasting it as a misunderstanding dodges ownership. Splitting the blame with a reviewer is technically true but sounds defensive.
questions.asked: Everyone has shipped a bug; interviewers want to see how you behave afterwards.

questions.q: A project you worked on for months was cancelled. Which answer best shows resilience and perspective?
choices: "I was very upset, and honestly I lost a lot of motivation for the next few months after it happened."
"It was frustrating, but user tests showed low demand, so stopping was right, and I reused the auth work."
"It showed that management had no real idea what they were doing, so I started looking around for other jobs."
"It did not bother me at all, since I get paid the same whether a project ships or gets cancelled."
questions.why: Acknowledging the frustration, understanding the business reason and salvaging something useful shows resilience. Losing motivation for months is honest but shows no recovery. Blaming management and job-hunting suggests you will not cope with normal business changes. Not caring at all suggests you are not invested in outcomes.
questions.asked: Priorities change; interviewers want to know you will not take it personally.

questions.q: Your estimate for a feature was off by 100%. Which answer best shows you learned from it?
choices: "I compared estimate to actual, saw I had missed integration work, and now list integrations up front."
"Estimates are always wrong, so I have stopped worrying about them and focus on the work itself."
"I now double every estimate I give, so that I will never be caught out by the same thing again."
"The requirements changed halfway through the work, so the estimate was not really wrong at the time I made it."
questions.why: Learning from an estimate miss means finding which part you underestimated and changing how you estimate. Giving up on estimates ignores why the team needs them. Doubling everything hides the cause and makes plans less useful. Blaming changed requirements may be partly true but offers no learning.
questions.asked: Estimation misses are universal; the specific cause you found is what interviewers want.

questions.q: You accidentally deleted rows from a staging database other teams were using. Which answer best shows immediate ownership?
choices: "I quietly restored it from last night's backup myself and hoped that nobody had noticed anything missing."
"I waited to see whether anyone would complain before deciding whether it needed to be fixed."
"I told my manager, and let them decide whether the other teams needed to know about it."
"I posted in the shared channel straight away, restored from backup, and added a guard on that script."
questions.why: Telling the affected teams immediately lets them avoid wasting time on odd results, and the guard stops a repeat. Restoring quietly still leaves people debugging missing data they do not know about. Waiting for complaints puts the cost on others. Passing the decision to your manager delays the people who need to know.
questions.asked: Speed and openness after a mistake matter more than the mistake itself.

questions.q: You are on call and paged at 2 a.m. for an alert you do not recognise. Which answer best shows calm, effective handling?
choices: "I started changing configuration until the alert cleared, since speed was the most important thing."
"I silenced the alert and went back to sleep, planning to look into it properly in the morning."
"I checked the runbook, confirmed user impact on the dashboard, mitigated, and escalated where unsure."
"I woke up the whole team straight away, since it is always better to have everyone on it together."
questions.why: A calm sequence is: find guidance, check real impact, mitigate, and escalate if out of depth. Silencing without checking risks a real outage going unnoticed. Changing configuration blindly can make things worse and destroys evidence. Waking everyone for an unknown alert burns the team out and is what escalation policies are for.
questions.asked: Tests how you behave under pressure, which on-call shows quickly.

questions.q: You have three deadlines in the same week. Which answer best shows how you manage competing commitments?
choices: "I worked on all three a little each day, so that every one of them moved forward at the same pace."
"I listed them with their impact, told each requester what was realistic, and did them in order."
"I worked until midnight all week and got them all done, because that is what commitment means."
"I did the easiest one first to get a quick win, then worried about the other two afterwards."
questions.why: Ranking by impact and telling each requester the realistic timing lets them plan, and doing one at a time finishes things. Spreading effort across all three risks finishing none. Working until midnight is a short-term fix that hides a capacity problem. Easiest-first optimises for your feeling of progress, not for the business.
questions.asked: Workload questions test whether you communicate before you fall behind.

questions.q: A colleague asks you to help cover up a mistake they made in production. Which answer best shows integrity while staying supportive?
choices: "I said I could not hide it, offered to help fix it, and went with them to explain it to the lead."
"I reported them to our manager straight away, without speaking to them about it first at all."
"I refused and then told the rest of the team about it, so that everyone knew what had happened."
"I helped them hide it, since reporting it would only get them into trouble for no real benefit."
questions.why: Integrity means not concealing an incident, and support means helping them fix it and face it. Hiding it risks customers and trust, and makes you complicit. Reporting without speaking to them first damages the relationship unnecessarily. Telling the whole team humiliates them and is gossip, not accountability.
questions.asked: Integrity questions have a clear right answer; interviewers watch how you handle the human side.

questions.q: Asked "Why are you leaving your current job?", which answer is most positive and forward-looking?
choices: "I have learned a lot there, but I want to work on a product with real scale and more backend ownership."
"My manager is difficult and the codebase is a total mess, so honestly I just need to get out of there."
"Mainly the money, to be honest; I have heard this company pays quite a bit more than where I am now."
"I am not really sure; I just feel it is time for something different, whatever that turns out to be."
questions.why: A strong answer credits your current role and points towards something this job offers. Criticising your manager and codebase makes the interviewer wonder what you will say about them. Leading with money is honest but suggests you will leave for the next offer. Having no idea what you want makes it hard to see why this role fits.
questions.asked: Interviewers listen for whether you are running away from something or towards something.

questions.q: Asked "Where do you see yourself in three years?", which answer best shows ambition aligned with the role?
choices: "I do not really plan that far ahead in my career, so I would rather just see what happens and take it as it comes."
"Honestly, I would like to have your job by then, since management is where I think I really belong."
"Probably running my own startup, as I see this role mainly as a chance to learn how companies work."
"Owning a significant part of the system, mentoring newer developers, and leading small projects end to end."
questions.why: The best answer describes growth the company can offer inside the job you are applying for: deeper ownership, mentoring, leading work. Aiming for the interviewer's job sounds either naive or combative. Planning to leave for a startup signals a short tenure. Having no plan suggests low motivation to grow.
questions.asked: Companies invest in people they expect to grow with them; this checks for fit.

questions.q: You moved into software from teaching via a bootcamp. Which answer best frames the career change as a strength?
choices: "I know I am behind people with CS degrees, so I hope you will give me a chance and be a bit patient with me."
"Teaching was not for me, as the pay was poor and the hours were long, so I needed a totally new start."
"Teaching taught me to explain clearly and plan under pressure; I use both when writing docs and reviews."
"My background is irrelevant now, since all that really matters in this job is how well I can code."
questions.why: Framing a career change well links skills from the old career to concrete behaviours in the new one. Apologising for lacking a degree invites the interviewer to see you as a risk. Explaining why you left teaching focuses on the negative. Calling your background irrelevant throws away the thing that makes you different from other candidates.
questions.asked: Career changers are common; interviewers want to know what you bring, not what you lack.

questions.q: Asked about a nine-month gap in your CV, which answer is most honest and reassuring?
choices: "I would rather not go into it, as it was a personal matter and I do not think it is relevant here."
"I cared for a parent, then built two projects to refresh my skills; that is behind me and I am ready."
"I was busy with lots of different things, and I was also doing some freelance work here and there."
"It was a hard job market, and nobody was hiring, so there was really nothing much I could do about it."
questions.why: A brief, honest reason, what you did to stay current and a clear statement that you are ready answers the real concern, which is whether you can start fully. Refusing outright raises more questions than it avoids, although you need not share private detail. Vague freelance claims invite probing you may not survive. Blaming the market sounds passive.
questions.asked: Gaps are common; interviewers mostly want to hear that you are ready now.

questions.q: Your manager pushes to skip tests to hit a demo date. Which answer best shows you can balance quality and speed?
choices: "I tested the payment path fully, left the admin screens lighter, and logged a ticket for the rest."
"I skipped all of the tests as asked, since the manager is responsible for any risk that follows."
"I refused to write any code without full test coverage, as quality should never be compromised."
"I wrote the tests secretly after hours, so that the manager would not know I was slowing things down."
questions.why: Balancing speed and quality means testing where failure is expensive, accepting risk where it is cheap, and recording the debt. Refusing all compromise ignores a real business date. Skipping everything and blaming the manager abdicates your professional judgement. Working secretly after hours hides the trade-off instead of discussing it.
